newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU plans to make polluters pay.
newsitem.headline: EU plans to make polluters pay.

text.p: European Commission plans to make polluting industries responsible for the cost of cleaning up any mess they make came a step closer to fruition on Wednesday as the executive agreed to draw up binding rules.
"The outcome of the discussion in the Commission was that a white paper is going to be issued," Commission spokesman Nikolaus van der Pas told a news conference.
Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard, who would be responsible for the drafting the planned paper on environmental liability, did not say how long this would take.

The paper would lay out three options for an EU-level legal instrument on liability, ranging from a directive for a general liability law, EU accession to the Council of Europe's Lugano Convention on liability or a narrower directive covering environmental damage alone.

"During the discussions in the Commission it became clear that it is a very complicated decision. Member states are not all that enthusiastic and there are major reservations in industry. Nevertheless, it's clear that something has to be done," van der Pas said.

A Bjerregaard document prepared ahead of Wednesday's meeting said five countries -- Finland, Greece, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands -- had already signed the Lugano Convention while Austria had drafted broadly similar national laws. It suggested that the EU join the Convention as a way to harmonise the national laws of all 15 EU countries.

In contrast, Germany, Britain, Denmark and France were "known to oppose the approach" mapped out in the Convention, the first three because of conflicts with their national laws and the latter because of questions about giving the Commission greater powers. Britain also shared France's position.

The Commission has been down this road before, unsuccessfully launching in 1993 a plan for a dual EU-level civil liability regime combining a strict, no-fault liability system with a compensation system for cases when damage could not be attributed to anyone.
Even Bjerregaard's officials were cautious on Wednesday about the chances of progress.
"The Commission has passed the point of no return, it will have to deal with liability. I think we will aim to do that as quickly as possible," one official told Reuters.
"I am not sure exactly what action the white paper will contain. It will be a proposal for concrete action," he said.
